UNIT.subject: Biology
UNIT.strand: Strand 2.0: Anatomy and Physiology of Plants
UNIT.content:
• Asexual reproduction in plants: sporulation and vegetative propagation
• Specialised vegetative structures: runners, bulbs, corms, rhizomes, offshoots, tubers, and cuttings
• Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
• Identification of flowers based on position of the ovary (superior/inferior), symmetry, inflorescence, and presence of male and female parts
• Mechanisms and features that hinder self-pollination and self-fertilisation (protandry, protogyny, heterostyly, dioecy, self-incompatibility)
• Double fertilisation and its significance
• Seed and fruit development including placentation (marginal, axile, parietal, free-central) and classification of fruits
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) Describe asexual reproduction in plants.
b) Identify flowers based on their floral parts.
c) Illustrate mechanisms and features that hinder self-pollination and self-fertilisation in plants.
d) Describe the process of double fertilisation in flowering plants.
e) Acknowledge the importance of sexual and asexual reproduction in plants.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Communication and Collaboration: The learner cooperates with others while observing and classifying specimens of flowers from different plants (Lessons 1 & 2), sharing observations and co-constructing understanding through structured group discussion and peer presentation.
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: The learner analyses causes and effects while brainstorming on the advantages and disadvantages of sexual and asexual reproduction in plants (Lesson 6), evaluating trade-offs using evidence from local agricultural case studies such as banana wilt disease and seed crop variation.
UNIT.values:
• Social Justice: The learner shares resources equitably while examining, drawing, and labelling sections of fruits (Lesson 5), ensuring all group members access dissecting equipment and fruit specimens fairly during practical work.
• Love: The learner prioritises others' interests while using models and charts to illustrate mechanisms and features that hinder self-pollination and self-fertilisation in plants (Lesson 3), patiently supporting peers to understand structural adaptations through collaborative model-building activities.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions and Defining Problems: Learners generate and refine questions for the Driving Question Board across all lessons, particularly in Lessons 1 and 2, identifying what puzzles them about why cassava and sweet potato propagate without seeds while maize requires pollination.
• Planning and Carrying Out Investigations: Learners plan and execute dissection of local flower specimens (Hibiscus, passion flower, maize) and fruit sections (tomato, orange, bean pod) in Lessons 2 and 5 to gather structural evidence.
• Analyzing and Interpreting Data: Learners examine and classify floral and fruit specimens, record observations in labelled diagrams, and interpret placentation patterns in Lessons 2 and 5.
• Developing and Using Models: Learners construct and iteratively revise physical and diagrammatic models of asexual structures, floral adaptations, and double fertilisation pathways across Lessons 1, 3, 4, and 7.
• Constructing Explanations: Learners build Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) written explanations in Lesson 8 that synthesise all unit evidence to answer the driving question.
• Engaging in Argument from Evidence: Learners conduct a structured debate on the agricultural and ecological trade-offs of sexual versus asexual reproduction in Lesson 6, using case study cards as evidence.
UNIT.pcis:
• Environment and Technology: The learner appreciates the use of technology in managing the environment while watching animations illustrating double fertilisation and formation of seeds and fruits (Lesson 4), connecting digital visualisation tools to understanding how crop fruit-set can be managed in Kenyan agriculture.
• Online Safety: The learner explores safe internet sites while watching animations illustrating double fertilisation and formation of seeds and fruits (Lesson 4), guided by the teacher to use only KICD-approved and vetted online resources accessed via a pre-downloaded cache where connectivity is limited.
UNIT.careers:
• Agronomist: Understands vegetative propagation techniques and cross-pollination requirements to advise Kenyan farmers on cassava, sugarcane, and avocado production.
• Plant Breeder: Applies knowledge of self-incompatibility, double fertilisation, and genetic variation from sexual reproduction to develop improved crop varieties for Kenyan conditions.
• Agricultural Extension Officer: Uses understanding of both sexual and asexual reproduction to train smallholder farmers in the Rift Valley and Western Kenya on optimal planting and propagation methods.
• Botanist: Classifies and studies flower morphology, fruit structure, and placentation types as part of plant taxonomy and ecological research in Kenyan biodiversity hotspots.
• Horticulturalist: Applies vegetative propagation skills (cuttings, grafting, runners) and knowledge of pollination requirements for fruit crops such as passion fruit and avocado grown across Kenya.
• Crop Geneticist: Investigates mechanisms preventing self-fertilisation and designs cross-breeding programmes to improve yield and disease resistance in Kenyan staple crops.
UNIT.focus: This unit anchors learning in the observable puzzle of why Kenyan smallholder farmers successfully propagate cassava, sweet potato, and sugarcane from cuttings and tubers without any seeds, while a solitary pawpaw or avocado tree flowers abundantly yet fails to set fruit without a neighbouring tree. Students build understanding progressively — from asexual structures and flower morphology through mechanisms preventing self-fertilisation, double fertilisation, and fruit development — using local plant specimens, physical models, and digital animations. The unit culminates in students constructing evidence-based explanations that connect crop propagation practices to fundamental plant reproductive biology, equipping them with knowledge directly applicable to Kenyan agricultural contexts.
UNIT.phenomenon: Farmers across Kenya — in Murang'a, Kisii, and the Coastal lowlands — routinely cut a piece of cassava stem, push it into the soil, and weeks later a new plant emerges. Sweet potato vines are snipped and replanted; sugarcane setts sprout into full stands; onion bulbs split and multiply — all without a single seed being planted. Yet when the same farmers plant a lone pawpaw tree or a solitary avocado in their compound, the tree flowers profusely season after season but the flowers drop off and no fruit develops, unless a second tree is planted nearby. Students encounter this contrast daily — buying seedless-propagated cassava flour and avocado from the same market — yet cannot explain why the biology of propagation is so different across these common crops. This is puzzling because if plants can reproduce without seeds, why do some plants absolutely need flowers, pollen from another individual, and fertilisation just to make a single fruit? The phenomenon invites students to investigate the full spectrum of plant reproductive strategies and the structural, chemical, and temporal mechanisms that govern them.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A student notices that the bryophyllum (resurrection plant / izwe) growing along a Nairobi school fence produces tiny plantlets along the edges of its leaves that drop off and root independently — raising the question of how a leaf can become a new plant without flowers or seeds.
• A tea farmer in Kericho observes that tea estates propagate millions of identical bushes from stem cuttings rather than seeds, yet wild tea plants produce flowers and berries — prompting the question of why the farmer avoids seed propagation if seeds are available.
• A passion fruit grower near Thika notices that vines grown from cuttings flower well but produce little fruit when isolated, while vines in a shared plot with other individuals fruit heavily — connecting to mechanisms that prevent self-fertilisation in passion flowers.
• A maize farmer in the Rift Valley observes that maize plants have separate tassel (male) and ear (female) structures on the same plant, yet wind still carries pollen between different plants — raising the question of whether structural separation alone is sufficient to prevent self-pollination.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: Why do some farm plants produce offspring without seeds while others require seeds and a partner tree to make fruit?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. What is the significance of reproduction in plants?
2. How does reproduction occur in plants?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Students are presented with the anchoring phenomenon (cassava cuttings vs. lone pawpaw) and examine local asexual propagation specimens — sweet potato tubers, onion bulbs, ginger rhizomes, grass runners, and bryophyllum leaves — to discover that plants can reproduce through specialised vegetative structures and sporulation without forming seeds; students record initial models and populate the Driving Question Board with their first questions.
Lesson 2: Students examine, dissect, and classify real flower specimens (Hibiscus, Bougainvillea, maize inflorescence, passion flower) to identify floral parts and distinguish flowers by ovary position (superior/inferior), symmetry (actinomorphic/zygomorphic), inflorescence type, and presence of male and female organs — discovering that not all flowers share the same structure; the DQB is updated with questions about self-pollination.
Lesson 3: Students use physical wire-and-bead models and structural charts to simulate and illustrate the specific mechanisms and features — protandry, protogyny, heterostyly, dioecy, and self-incompatibility — that prevent self-pollination and self-fertilisation in plants such as avocado and passion fruit, directly connecting to why the lone pawpaw tree in the phenomenon fails to fruit; groups present their models to peers.
Lesson 4: Students watch pre-downloaded KICD-approved digital animations of pollen tube growth and double fertilisation, then trace and diagram the pathway — one sperm nucleus fusing with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote, another fusing with polar nuclei to form a triploid endosperm — in their workbooks; the lesson links fertilisation success to seed and fruit formation, advancing understanding of why cross-pollination is necessary in the phenomenon crops.
Lesson 5: Students section, examine, draw, and label local fruits — orange (axile placentation), bean pod (marginal placentation), tomato (axile), passion fruit (parietal), cucumber (parietal) — to classify placentation types and understand seed arrangement as evidence of fertilisation and ovary development; resources are shared equitably across groups of 4–5, embedding the Social Justice value.
Lesson 6: Students conduct a structured brainstorm and evidence-based debate comparing the advantages and disadvantages of sexual reproduction (genetic variation, disease resilience) and asexual reproduction (rapid identical replication, no pollinator needed) using case study cards on banana wilt (a disease devastating clonally propagated banana plantations in Kenya) versus maize seed diversity — synthesising why both strategies are valuable in nature and Kenyan agriculture.
Lesson 7: Students return to their original Lesson 1 models, revise them in light of all accumulated evidence, and present group explanatory models connecting vegetative structures, floral adaptations, anti-self-pollination mechanisms, double fertilisation, and fruit development; sticky notes on the DQB are reviewed and answered, and students identify any remaining questions for the final lesson.
Lesson 8: Students individually complete a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) written explanation answering the driving question — why some farm plants reproduce without seeds while others require cross-pollination to set fruit — followed by a peer-review process and a formative/summative unit assessment; the unit closes by connecting student understanding to careers in agronomy, plant breeding, and horticulture in Kenya.

slo.purpose: To launch the anchoring phenomenon and establish that plants can reproduce without seeds through specialised vegetative structures and sporulation, while raising the question of why other plants require flowers and a second individual to fruit.
slo.knowledge: Students will identify and describe asexual reproduction in plants, including sporulation and vegetative propagation through specialised structures such as runners, bulbs, corms, rhizomes, tubers, and cuttings.
slo.skills: Students will observe, handle, and classify local plant specimens; draw and annotate initial conceptual models; and construct questions for the Driving Question Board.
slo.attitudes: Students will acknowledge the importance of asexual reproduction in everyday Kenyan agriculture and appreciate how indigenous farming knowledge connects to biological science.
slo.keyInquiry: What is the significance of reproduction in plants?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This opening lesson anchors the entire sub-strand by presenting the contrast between seed-free propagation (cassava cuttings, sweet potato vines, onion bulbs) and the frustrated fruiting of a lone pawpaw. Students gather physical evidence from local specimens and build their first explanatory model, populating the Driving Question Board with questions that will drive inquiry across subsequent lessons on sexual reproduction, floral structure, pollination mechanisms, double fertilisation, and fruit development.
slo.safetyNotes: No cutting instruments are used in this lesson. All specimens are handled intact or pre-sectioned by the teacher before class. Students wash hands after handling soil-covered specimens. Remind students not to put any plant material near their eyes or mouth. Students with known plant allergies should inform the teacher before handling specimens. Lab safety protocols involving mounted dissecting blades and razors are formally introduced in Lesson 2.

LESSONS.overview: Students are drawn into the anchoring phenomenon through a brief teacher-narrated story about farmers in Murang'a planting cassava stems and in Mombasa watching a lone pawpaw tree flower and drop its fruits season after season. Working in groups of four to five, students examine a tray of local asexual propagation specimens — sweet potato tubers, onion bulbs, ginger rhizomes, Kikuyu grass runners, and bryophyllum leaves with plantlets — and use hand lenses to observe the structural features that allow each specimen to produce a new plant without seeds. Each group produces a classification table and shares one 'surprising observation' with the class. In the Explain phase, students apply Claim-Evidence-Reasoning to state what they now believe about plant reproduction without seeds. The lesson closes with students drawing their first initial conceptual model comparing a sweet potato tuber producing a vine to a bean seed producing a plant, then writing their burning questions on sticky notes and pinning them to the Driving Question Board under two columns: 'Without Seeds' and 'With Seeds'.

framework.learnerExperience: Students listen to a short teacher-narrated scenario: a farmer in Murang'a cuts a cassava stem, pushes it into the soil, and three weeks later a new plant is growing — no seed was ever planted. The same farmer plants a single pawpaw seedling, it grows tall, flowers abundantly every season, but every flower drops without producing a single fruit. Students are then given 3 minutes of silent thinking time before writing their answers individually on a half-sheet of paper: (1) How do you think the cassava stem grew into a new plant? (2) Why do you think the lone pawpaw tree never produces fruit? Students are not told whether their predictions are correct — these papers are collected and returned at the end of the sub-strand as evidence of growth.
framework.teacherMoves: Narrate the scenario with energy: 'Imagine you are a farmer in Murang'a. You cut a cassava stem — no root, no seed, just a stick — push it into the soil, and three weeks later green leaves are pushing out of the ground. How is that possible?' Pause for 10 seconds of WAIT TIME. Then say: 'Now picture a farmer in Mombasa with a lone pawpaw tree in their compound. The tree flowers every season — beautiful yellow flowers — but not a single fruit forms. Why?' Pause again for 12 seconds of WAIT TIME. Distribute the prediction half-sheets. After 3 minutes of silent writing, cold-call 3 students to share predictions — select one who seems confident, one who looks uncertain, and one who has written a lot. Record key prediction phrases on the board under two columns: 'CASSAVA — no seed needed' and 'PAWPAW — flowers but no fruit'. Do not correct students. Say: 'We are going to hold these ideas and test them against evidence today and across many lessons. Let us see how your thinking changes.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) — Predict stage. By articulating predictions before encountering evidence, students activate prior knowledge from everyday agricultural observations, create cognitive dissonance that motivates inquiry, and establish a personal baseline that makes conceptual change visible by the end of the sub-strand.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect prediction half-sheets. Scan for: (1) whether students distinguish between vegetative and seed-based reproduction using any vocabulary; (2) whether students link the lone pawpaw's failure to the absence of a second tree or to pollination. These baseline responses inform which misconceptions to address in subsequent lessons. Observable indicator: every student has written at least one sentence for each question before sheets are collected.

framework.learnerExperience: Students first do a 3-minute Think-Pair-Share: Think individually — 'Based on what you just observed, what do all these specimens have in common that allows them to make a new plant?' Pair with the person next to them for 2 minutes. Share with the whole class. Following the share-out, the teacher introduces the biological vocabulary for each structure — runner, bulb, corm, rhizome, tuber, cutting, sporulation (using bryophyllum as the entry point for sporulation, noting that bryophyllum produces plantlets that drop and root, functioning analogously to spores in the broader sense of asexual dispersal units) — connecting each term to the specimen students held. Students then individually apply the Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) framework in their notebooks by completing a structured sentence frame: 'CLAIM: Plants can reproduce without seeds because... EVIDENCE: When I observed [specimen], I noticed [specific structure]... REASONING: This shows that [biological explanation]...' Groups have 6 minutes to write individual CERs, after which two students are cold-called to read their CER aloud and the class gives one piece of peer feedback using the sentence starter 'I agree with your evidence because... / I would add to your reasoning...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Launch Think-Pair-Share by saying: 'Before I give you any vocabulary, I want you to figure out the pattern from your own evidence. Think silently for one minute — what do ALL five specimens have in common?' Allow exactly 60 seconds of WAIT TIME. Then: 'Turn to your partner. You have 2 minutes.' Circulate and listen for the word 'buds', 'nodes', 'stored food', or 'already has parts'. After pairs share, introduce vocabulary deliberately slowly, pointing to each specimen as you say each term: 'The ginger structure is called a rhizome — an underground stem that stores food and has nodes that sprout. The onion is a bulb — layers of modified leaves around a central bud. The grass structure showing roots at intervals is called a runner or stolon.' Write each term on the board next to a simple sketch. For bryophyllum, say: 'This one is particularly fascinating — tiny complete plantlets form along the leaf margin. This is related to a type of asexual reproduction called sporulation. The plantlets drop to the soil and root independently.' For CER, say: 'Now I want you to make a scientific claim and back it up with your own evidence from the tray. Use this sentence frame.' Write the frame on the board. After 6 minutes, cold-call 2 students. After each CER, ask: 'Class — one piece of feedback using the sentence starter on the board. Count of 10 seconds, then I will cold-call.' Allow 10 seconds of WAIT TIME before cold-calling feedback.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) framework. CER moves students from observation to explanation by requiring them to explicitly link a biological claim to physical evidence and a reasoning chain. In this lesson, the CER anchors vocabulary learning to specimen evidence rather than rote definition, building the habit of evidence-based explanation that will be used throughout the sub-strand including when analysing double fertilisation and fruit classification in later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Read CER entries as students write. Observable indicators of proficiency: (1) the CLAIM names at least one type of asexual reproduction; (2) the EVIDENCE cites a specific specimen by name and a specific structure observed; (3) the REASONING connects the structure to function (e.g., 'the bud on the tuber already contains meristematic tissue that can develop into a shoot'). Students who write only general claims without specimen evidence are flagged for additional support in the next lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: Each student receives two sticky notes. On the first sticky note, they write one question about how plants reproduce WITHOUT seeds that this lesson has not yet answered. On the second sticky note, they write one question about how plants reproduce WITH seeds, flowers, or fruit — anything the phenomenon has made them curious about. Students pin their sticky notes on the class Driving Question Board, a large sheet of chart paper divided into two columns: 'Without Seeds' and 'With Seeds'. The teacher reads five questions aloud — two from the 'Without Seeds' column and three from the 'With Seeds' column — chosen to represent a range of thinking levels. The class votes with a show of hands on which 'With Seeds' question they are MOST curious about. This winning question is circled and labelled 'Our Priority Question for the next lessons.'
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute sticky notes and say: 'This board will grow across every lesson in this sub-strand. Every question you pin is a real scientific question that biologists have investigated. Today is Day 1 — we are opening the board.' Give students 3 minutes to write both sticky notes in silence. Circulate to ensure students are writing questions not statements. If a student writes 'Plants reproduce using tubers' redirect: 'That is a statement. Can you turn it into a question — what is something about tubers you still do not understand?' After pinning, read the five selected questions aloud with genuine enthusiasm. For the vote, say: 'Raise your hand for the question you most want to answer over the next lessons. Keep your hand up until I count — 3, 2, 1, hands down.' Circle the winning question visibly in red marker. Say: 'This question is going to drive our investigation in Lessons 2 through 5. Every time we find new evidence, we will come back to this board and update our thinking.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (DQB). The DQB externalises student curiosity and makes the class's collective knowledge gaps visible. By organising questions under 'Without Seeds' and 'With Seeds', students themselves articulate the central contrast of the anchoring phenomenon. Returning to the DQB in every subsequent lesson creates a through-line of inquiry ownership, reinforcing that science is a process of progressively answering questions rather than memorising fixed answers.
framework.formativeAssessment: Read all sticky notes after class. Observable indicators: (1) questions are genuinely interrogative; (2) at least 70% of 'With Seeds' questions reference flowers, pollen, fruit, or a second plant — indicating students have connected the lone pawpaw observation to a need for a partner; (3) fewer than 20% of questions are already answered by today's lesson (indicating appropriate calibration of what they know vs. what they still need to figure out). Questions that reveal deep misconceptions (e.g., 'Does a mango tree need to be married to another tree?') are noted for explicit address in Lesson 3 on pollination mechanisms.

framework.learnerExperience: Students open their biology notebooks to a fresh page headed 'My Initial Model — Lesson 1'. They draw two side-by-side diagrams: LEFT diagram — a sweet potato tuber in soil producing a new vine (labelled with what they now know about the structure that enables this). RIGHT diagram — a bean seed in soil producing a new plant (labelled with what they remember about seed germination from earlier learning). Beneath both diagrams, students write one sentence explaining: 'The key difference I notice between these two ways of starting a new plant is...' Students are explicitly told these models are not graded — they are a record of their thinking TODAY, and they will revise them in every subsequent lesson as their understanding grows.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Scientists do not just write notes — they build models. A model is a diagram that shows what you THINK is happening and WHY. Your model does not have to be perfect. In fact, today's model is supposed to be incomplete because we are just beginning.' Write on the board: 'LEFT: Sweet potato tuber → new vine. RIGHT: Bean seed → new plant.' Say: 'Label everything you know. If you are unsure of a label, write a question mark. Question marks in your model are honest science.' Give 7 minutes for drawing. At the 4-minute mark, circulate and offer a specific prompt to any student drawing only surface features: 'Can you show WHERE on the tuber the new shoot comes from? Is there a specific structure?' With 1 minute remaining, say: 'Write your one sentence about the key difference. This is your scientific thinking today — it will change and that is the whole point.' Collect no notebooks — students keep their models for revision in future lessons.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial model building. Drawing an explanatory model requires students to integrate observational evidence (from the specimen tray) with prior knowledge (bean seed germination) and make their reasoning visible in spatial form. The side-by-side format creates an explicit structural comparison that will grow into a full mechanistic model of both asexual and sexual reproduction by the end of the sub-strand. Labelled question marks normalise uncertainty as part of scientific practice.
framework.formativeAssessment: Circulate during model building and conduct 3 oral probes with individual students: 'Show me in your diagram where exactly the new plant comes from on the sweet potato.' Observable indicators of understanding: (1) students draw a bud or 'eye' on the tuber as the origin of the new shoot; (2) students label stored food/starch in the tuber; (3) students show the vine emerging from a specific point rather than randomly from the tuber surface. Students who draw the tuber as simply 'a big seed' have a persistent misconception to address in Lesson 2 — note their names for targeted questioning.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following: (1) Which prediction on the half-sheets surprised you most — what does it tell you about students' agricultural knowledge versus their biological understanding? (2) During the specimen observation, which structure caused the most confusion — was it the runner (often confused with a root), the rhizome (often confused with a root too), or the bryophyllum plantlets? Plan a 5-minute clarification at the start of Lesson 2 if more than one-third of groups struggled with the same specimen. (3) Review the DQB sticky notes: Are most 'With Seeds' questions about flowers, about the second pawpaw tree, or about something unexpected? The pattern of questions should shape how much time you allocate to floral structure in Lesson 2. (4) Were groups of 4–5 functioning productively, or did one student dominate the hand lens? Consider assigning rotating roles (Lens Holder, Recorder, Reporter, Time Keeper) from Lesson 2 onward to ensure equitable participation across all 45–50 students. (5) Note any student who drew the tuber as 'a big seed' in their initial model — these students need the conceptual distinction between a seed (embryo + endosperm + seed coat, result of sexual reproduction) and a vegetative storage organ (result of mitotic growth) addressed explicitly before Lesson 3.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed sweet potato tubers, onion bulbs, ginger rhizomes, Kikuyu grass runners, and bryophyllum leaves with plantlets. None of these specimens contained seeds, yet Kenyan farmers use all of them to produce new plants.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Plants can reproduce asexually through specialised vegetative structures (runners, bulbs, corms, rhizomes, tubers, cuttings) and through sporulation (as seen in bryophyllum), all without forming seeds. These structures contain stored nutrients and meristematic tissue capable of producing a new genetically identical plant.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: This explains why a Murang'a farmer can push a cassava stem into the soil and grow a new plant — the stem already contains the structures and stored energy needed to produce roots and shoots without fertilisation. However, it does NOT yet explain why the lone pawpaw tree in Mombasa flowers but never fruits, which is the question driving our next lessons on sexual reproduction in flowering plants.

LESSONS.title: Flower Anatomy and Classification: Why Aren't All Flowers the Same?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: floral parts, ovary position, superior ovary, inferior ovary, actinomorphic, zygomorphic, inflorescence, bisexual flower, unisexual flower, floral dissection, Hibiscus, Bougainvillea, maize, passion flower

slo.purpose: Students examine and dissect real flower specimens to identify floral parts and classify flowers by ovary position, symmetry, inflorescence type, and presence of male and female organs, building evidence that flower structure varies across plant species.
slo.knowledge: Students will know: (a) the names and functions of floral parts (sepals, petals, stamens, pistil, receptacle, peduncle); (b) the distinction between superior and inferior ovary positions; (c) the difference between actinomorphic and zygomorphic symmetry; (d) types of inflorescence (solitary, raceme, spike, panicle); (e) the difference between bisexual and unisexual flowers; and (f) how flower structure relates to the phenomenon of why some plants need a partner to produce fruit.
slo.skills: Students will be able to: (a) safely dissect flower specimens using razor blades and hand lenses; (b) identify and label floral parts on a diagram; (c) classify flowers based on observable structural features; (d) construct a floral classification table using evidence from dissection; and (e) pose evidence-based questions for the Driving Question Board.
slo.attitudes: Students will: (a) appreciate the diversity of flower structures as adaptations shaped by millions of years of evolution; (b) work collaboratively and share dissecting equipment equitably (Social Justice value — KICD); (c) prioritise group learning by listening to peers during classification discussions (Love value — KICD); and (d) develop curiosity about how structural differences in flowers might explain fruit production patterns observed in Kenyan farms.
slo.keyInquiry: How does reproduction occur in plants? (KICD Key Inquiry Question 2) — specifically, how does the structural variety of flowers relate to how plants are fertilised and produce fruit?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1, students established that cassava, sweet potato, and sugarcane reproduce vegetatively without seeds or flowers. Lesson 2 shifts the lens to sexual reproduction by asking: what is a flower and why does its structure matter? By dissecting Hibiscus, Bougainvillea, maize inflorescences, and passion flowers, students gather direct evidence that not all flowers share the same design — some have both male and female parts, others do not; some ovaries sit above the petals, others below. This structural diversity becomes the foundation for the next inquiry: if a flower has both male and female parts, why does it not always pollinate itself? The DQB is updated with student-generated questions about self-pollination, directly advancing the driving question about why a lone pawpaw or avocado fails to fruit.
slo.safetyNotes: EXPLICIT LAB SAFETY PROTOCOLS (mandatory — read aloud before dissection begins): (1) Razor blades and mounted dissecting blades are to remain on the dissection tray at all times and must never be passed hand-to-hand between students — place the blade on the tray and allow the next student to pick it up. (2) Always cut away from the body, keeping the non-cutting hand behind the blade. (3) Broken or chipped blades must be reported to the teacher immediately and placed in the designated sharps container — never in the general waste bin. (4) Students with cuts or open wounds on their hands must wear gloves or be assigned a non-cutting role (observation and recording). (5) Hand lenses must be returned to the kit after use. (6) Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water after handling plant specimens, as some students may have pollen allergies. (7) Students who are known to have pollen allergies must inform the teacher before the lesson; they should wear a face mask and be seated away from the dissection station, taking on a recording/drawing role. (8) No eating or drinking during the practical session.

LESSONS.overview: Students begin by revisiting the Lesson 1 anchor phenomenon — farmers in Murang'a plant cassava cuttings and onion bulbs without seeds, yet a lone pawpaw in a Nairobi compound bears no fruit. The teacher poses the bridge question: 'If seeds come from flowers, what is inside a flower that makes the difference?' Students predict floral parts before dissection (Predict phase), then dissect four locally sourced specimens — Hibiscus, Bougainvillea, a maize cob/tassel, and passion flower — using razor blades and hand lenses in groups of 4–5 (Observe phase). Through a Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) cycle, students record observations and begin classifying flowers by ovary position, symmetry, inflorescence, and sexuality of floral parts (Explain phase). Groups then share their CER statements to the class. In the DQB phase, new student-generated questions — especially about self-pollination — are added to the board. Finally, students revise their cumulative models of plant reproduction, adding the sexual pathway and annotating it with the structural features they observed. Exit tickets check mastery of four floral classification criteria.

framework.learnerExperience: Students re-read the phenomenon statement displayed on the classroom wall: 'A farmer in Kisii plants cassava cuttings and harvests a crop. The same farmer plants one avocado tree in the compound — it flowers every season but never fruits. Why?' Students are then shown four whole, uncut flower specimens on a demonstration table (Hibiscus, Bougainvillea, one maize tassel, passion flower) and asked to write individual predictions in their notebooks: 'Sketch what you think is inside each flower. What parts does a flower need in order to make a fruit?' Students also answer: 'Do you think all four specimens have the same internal parts? Give a reason.' Predictions are written silently for 4 minutes before any peer discussion begins.
framework.teacherMoves: (1) Display the phenomenon statement and say verbatim: 'Last lesson we discovered that cassava and sweet potato can reproduce without flowers or seeds. Today we are going to look at the other side of that story — what happens inside a flower when a plant does need one to reproduce.' (2) Hold up each specimen in turn and ask: 'Take 10 seconds — just look. Do not touch yet.' [WAIT 10 seconds per specimen.] (3) Give the written prediction prompt orally and write it on the board: 'Sketch what you think is inside each flower. What parts does a flower need to make a fruit?' (4) Allow 4 minutes of silent individual prediction writing — circulate and note 3–4 interesting or misconception-revealing predictions to revisit later. (5) Cold-call 3 students: 'Wanjiku, tell me one part you drew and why you placed it there.' [WAIT 10 seconds after each name before accepting the answer.] (6) Do NOT correct predictions yet — affirm the thinking: 'Interesting — let's see whether the evidence agrees with you.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict Phase of POE (Predict-Observe-Explain): By committing predictions to paper before any instruction, students activate prior knowledge and create a cognitive stake in the outcome. When observations later contradict predictions, the cognitive dissonance drives deeper encoding of the correct concept. Teacher notes on student predictions also serve as a diagnostic tool for targeted questioning during the Explain phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Each student has a written sketch with at least one labelled part in their notebook before the group activity begins. Teacher circulates and stamps or initials notebooks that show a genuine attempt. Red flag: Students who draw nothing or write 'I don't know' are paired with a peer before dissection begins and given a printed reference silhouette of a generic flower to annotate.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4–5 students receive a dissection kit (razor blade in a mounted holder, hand lens, forceps, dissection tray, damp cloth) and one fresh specimen of each flower type — Hibiscus, Bougainvillea, maize tassel/young cob, and passion flower. The teacher reads the lab safety protocol aloud (see Safety Notes) and students sign the group safety agreement at the top of the worksheet. Students follow a structured dissection sequence on the Floral Classification Worksheet: (a) draw the whole flower before cutting; (b) remove sepals and petals carefully and lay them out on the tray; (c) locate and count stamens; (d) use the hand lens to identify the pistil (stigma, style, ovary); (e) make a longitudinal section through the ovary using the razor blade and observe ovule arrangement; (f) note ovary position relative to petals (superior or inferior); (g) observe symmetry by holding the cut flower at arm's length; (h) record all observations in the data table on the worksheet. Students photograph observations using any available phone camera (one per group) for reference during the Explain phase. Bougainvillea is included specifically to challenge students — its colourful 'petals' are actually bracts, and the true flower is tiny — creating productive cognitive conflict.
framework.teacherMoves: (1) Before distributing equipment: read the full safety protocol aloud, pause after each rule, and ask the class to repeat the most critical rule back: 'Everyone — what do we do with the blade when we want to pass it to a neighbour?' [WAIT 8 seconds, then accept choral response: 'Put it on the tray.'] (2) Demonstrate the longitudinal ovary cut on a spare Hibiscus at the front — narrate each step: 'I am pressing gently away from my fingers, keeping the blade on the tray surface.' (3) Circulate every 4 minutes. At each group ask one targeted probe: 'Can you show me the stigma? How do you know that is the stigma and not part of the style?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] (4) If a group finishes quickly, prompt extension: 'Compare your Hibiscus ovary section to the passion flower ovary — what is different about where the seeds are attached?' (5) Cold-call 4 different groups to report one surprising observation to the class: 'Group 3 — Achieng, what surprised your group about Bougainvillea?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] (6) At the 25-minute mark, call attention: 'Freeze — everyone put blades on the tray. Hold up your worksheet. You should have completed rows 1 and 2. If you have not, focus on the ovary section now — that is the most important structure for today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Observation with Guided Inquiry: The dissection worksheet scaffolds observation into discrete, ordered steps so that students are not overwhelmed by complexity. Laying excised parts on the tray creates a physical, spatial model of floral anatomy. The Bougainvillea 'false petal' discovery is a deliberate anomaly designed to produce cognitive conflict — when students realise what they called 'petals' are not petals at all, they must revise their definition of a flower, deepening conceptual understanding. Observation logs build the evidentiary foundation needed for the CER task in Phase 3.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Completed data table rows on the Floral Classification Worksheet — each row should have a sketch, a count of stamens, a note on ovary position (superior/inferior), and a note on symmetry. Teacher checks 5 random worksheets mid-dissection and gives verbal corrective feedback in under 30 seconds per group. Red flag: Groups that cannot locate the pistil in the Hibiscus — teacher redirects with the prompt: 'Look at the centre column. The sticky tip is the stigma. Follow it downward.'

framework.learnerExperience: Students transition from raw observation to classification and explanation. Using their completed dissection data, each group fills in the Floral Classification Summary Table: columns for Specimen, Ovary Position, Symmetry, Inflorescence Type, and Bisexual/Unisexual. Groups then construct a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statement for the following prompt, displayed on the board: 'CLAIM: All four flowers we dissected share the same internal structure. Do you AGREE or DISAGREE? Use EVIDENCE from your dissection and REASONING from what you know about reproduction to justify your answer.' Each group writes their CER on a shared A3 sheet. After 8 minutes of group work, a Think-Pair-Share is used: each student first writes their own version of the CER (2 minutes), then shares with the student next to them (2 minutes), then three groups present to the class. The teacher connects responses back to the phenomenon: 'So if maize has separate male and female flowers on the same plant, what does that tell us about whether it can self-pollinate? Think about that pawpaw in the Nairobi compound — might it have a similar situation?'
framework.teacherMoves: (1) Write the CER prompt on the board and model the structure: 'A CLAIM is a one-sentence answer. EVIDENCE is specific data from your dissection — number of stamens, position of ovary. REASONING explains why your evidence supports your claim using biology.' (2) Circulate during group CER writing. Target the Reasoning column: 'Your evidence says the ovary is inferior in passion flower — now WHY does that matter for how we classify it?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] (3) Use Think-Pair-Share transition: 'Stop. Write your own CER in your notebook — 2 minutes, individual, no talking.' [Set visible timer.] Then: 'Now turn to your neighbour and compare. Does your reasoning match theirs? You have 2 minutes.' (4) Cold-call 3 presenters — select one group with a correct CER, one with a partially correct CER, and one with a misconception: 'Group 7 — Mwenda, read your claim.' [WAIT 10 seconds.] After each, ask the class: 'Do you agree? Thumbs up or thumbs sideways.' (5) Address the maize inflorescence explicitly: 'Maize has two types of flowers — who can name them and where they sit on the plant? [WAIT 10 seconds.] The tassel at the top is the male inflorescence; the silk threads on the cob are the female flowers. What does this mean for self-pollination?' (6) Revisit predictions from Phase 1: 'Kamau predicted that all flowers have the same parts. What does our evidence say? Kamau, do you want to revise your prediction?' (7) Summarise the four classification criteria on the board as a class-constructed list: ovary position / symmetry / inflorescence type / bisexual or unisexual.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) Framework: CER pushes students beyond description ('the ovary is below the petals') to explanation ('therefore this is an inferior ovary, which means the ovary developed below the other floral parts and will form fruit differently'). The reasoning step explicitly connects structural evidence to the biological concept, mirroring the practices of working scientists. Think-Pair-Share amplifies individual accountability — students cannot rely on a group consensus without first formulating their own thinking. The teacher's deliberate selection of one correct, one partial, and one misconception CER for public presentation creates a low-stakes norm-setting moment where the class collectively refines scientific reasoning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) Each student's notebook contains an individual CER statement with all three components labelled. (b) The group A3 sheet correctly classifies at least 3 of 4 specimens in the summary table. (c) During cold-call presentations, the teacher uses a 3-point oral probe rubric: 1 = claim only, 2 = claim + evidence, 3 = claim + evidence + reasoning. Teacher records scores on a class roster. Red flag: A group that classifies Bougainvillea bracts as petals in their CER — teacher probes: 'Show me the bract and show me a petal from Hibiscus side by side. Are they the same structure?' to prompt self-correction.

framework.learnerExperience: Students are given two sticky notes each. On the first: 'Write one new question today's dissection made you think of.' On the second: 'Write what you now understand about flowers that you did NOT understand at the start of today's lesson.' Students post both notes on the class Driving Question Board under the headers 'NEW QUESTIONS' and 'WHAT WE NOW KNOW.' The teacher reads selected new questions aloud and groups them publicly into two clusters: (a) questions about self-pollination ('If a flower has both male and female parts, why doesn't pollen just fall onto the stigma of the same flower?'), and (b) questions about structure and function ('Why does the ovary position matter for the fruit shape?'). The teacher highlights the self-pollination cluster and tells the class: 'These are exactly the questions that biologists had to answer to explain why a lone pawpaw fails to fruit. We will investigate them in Lesson 3.' Students update the DQB model arrow: the sexual reproduction pathway now has a new node labelled 'FLOWER STRUCTURE — varies by ovary, symmetry, inflorescence, parts.'
framework.teacherMoves: (1) Distribute sticky notes and set a 3-minute individual writing timer: 'No talking — this is your individual thinking. One question per note, one new understanding per note.' (2) As students post notes, scan quickly and identify 2–3 self-pollination questions and 1–2 structure questions to read aloud: 'I see Otieno has written — and I am reading this exactly — 'If the stigma and stamens are in the same flower, why does pollen not just fall down?' That is a world-class scientific question. It goes in the self-pollination cluster.' (3) Point to the driving question on the wall: 'Why do some farm plants produce offspring without seeds while others require seeds and a partner tree to make fruit? — Otieno's question is starting to answer the second half of that. Hold onto it.' (4) Cold-call 2 students to read their 'WHAT WE NOW KNOW' sticky note aloud. Ask the class: 'Does everyone agree that belongs in the KNOW column, or is it still a question?' (5) Update the DQB model arrow explicitly: draw on the board and narrate — 'Our model of plant reproduction now has two pathways. Today we added detail to the sexual pathway — flowers are not all the same. That matters for what comes next.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (DQB) as a Living Knowledge Artefact: The DQB externalises the class's collective epistemic state — what is known, what is questioned, what is puzzling. By physically sorting new questions into clusters, the teacher models how scientists organise uncertainty into investigable sub-problems. The self-pollination cluster becomes the explicit bridge to Lesson 3, giving students a narrative throughline across the 8-lesson sequence. Students see their own questions shaping the direction of inquiry, which builds scientific agency and ownership of learning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every student has posted both sticky notes before the class timer ends. Teacher scans for blank or trivial questions ('What is a flower?') and redirects with: 'That is a good starting question — can you make it more specific? What did you see in the dissection that you cannot yet explain?' Red flag: Fewer than half the class posts a genuine self-pollination question — if this occurs, the teacher writes a model question on the board as a sentence starter: 'I wonder why a flower that has both _______ and _______ does not always _______..'

framework.learnerExperience: Students open their cumulative Plant Reproduction Model — started in Lesson 1 as a branching diagram with 'Asexual' and 'Sexual' pathways. They add a new annotated node to the Sexual pathway: a labelled floral diagram showing the four classification criteria (ovary position, symmetry, inflorescence, bisexual/unisexual) with an arrow connecting to 'Fruit/Seed production.' Students write a one-sentence model annotation: 'Flower structure varies across species because _______, and this matters for fruit production because _______.' Groups briefly compare their models with a neighbouring group (2 minutes) to check for missing labels. In the final 5 minutes, students complete the exit ticket individually on a half-sheet of paper: four fill-in questions, one per classification criterion, plus one phenomenon-link question: 'A farmer in Murang'a notices that her passion fruit vine flowers but produces no fruit. Based on today's lesson, name ONE structural feature of the flower she should investigate, and explain why that feature matters.'
framework.teacherMoves: (1) Direct students to open their Lesson 1 model: 'You have 8 minutes to add the flower structure node. It must have four labels — I will be checking every model.' (2) Circulate and use oral probes during model building: 'Show me where you wrote ovary position. Now tell me: is the Hibiscus ovary superior or inferior, and how do you know?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] (3) Peer comparison: 'Turn to the group next to you — you have 2 minutes. Check: do their four labels match yours? If they differ, decide together which is correct and why.' (4) Signal the transition to exit tickets: 'Models down, facing away. Exit ticket is individual — this is not group work. You have 5 minutes.' (5) Collect exit tickets at the door as students leave. Do a rapid sort into three piles: strong (correct phenomenon-link), developing (correct criteria but weak phenomenon-link), needs support (incomplete). Use this to plan Lesson 3 entry. (6) Close the lesson by connecting back to the driving question: 'Today you discovered that not all flowers are built the same way. Some have the ovary above the petals, some below; some have both male and female parts, some do not. Next lesson we will find out: if a flower has both male and female parts — like our Hibiscus — why doesn't it just pollinate itself and save the pawpaw farmer all that trouble?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: Revisiting and extending the same model across lessons makes scientific thinking visible as an evolving process rather than a fixed answer. Students see their understanding grow on paper, which reinforces metacognitive awareness. The model annotation sentence frame ('Flower structure varies because ___, and this matters for fruit production because ___') requires students to connect structural evidence to functional consequence — the core explanatory move of biology. Peer model comparison introduces a collaborative quality-control mechanism analogous to peer review in science.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) Exit ticket question 5 (phenomenon link) is answered with a specific structural feature (e.g., 'the farmer should check whether the passion flower is bisexual and whether the ovary position affects pollinator access') — teacher accepts any structurally grounded answer. (b) The cumulative model has four labelled criteria on the sexual pathway node. Teacher rapid-sorts exit tickets into three piles immediately after class; any student in the 'needs support' pile is given a 5-minute check-in at the start of Lesson 3 before new content begins. Red flag on exit ticket: Students who name 'colour of petals' as the key structural feature without mentioning ovary position, stamen/pistil presence, or symmetry — this indicates they observed surface features only and need targeted re-teaching in Lesson 3 on function over form.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) During the dissection, which specimen caused the most confusion — and did students resolve that confusion through peer talk or did they need teacher intervention? If Bougainvillea bracts consistently confused students, consider providing a labelled comparison card in future lessons. (2) How many of the DQB self-pollination questions were genuinely student-generated versus prompted by your model sentence starter? A higher ratio of prompted questions may indicate that students need more unstructured observation time before the DQB phase. (3) Review the exit ticket pile sorted into 'needs support': are these the same students who struggled in Lesson 1 with vegetative propagation, or are they different students? A pattern of different students struggling in different lessons suggests topic-specific gaps; the same students struggling suggests a foundational literacy or language barrier requiring differentiated support. (4) Did the 80-minute timeline hold? If Phase 2 (dissection) ran over time, consider pre-dissecting one specimen and leaving it open on the demonstration tray so that slower groups can reference a completed dissection rather than starting from scratch. (5) Safety check: Were all razor blades accounted for at the end of the lesson? Complete a blade count before dismissing the class — this is non-negotiable.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed four flower specimens — Hibiscus, Bougainvillea, maize inflorescence, and passion flower. We found that Hibiscus has a superior ovary, actinomorphic symmetry, and is bisexual; Bougainvillea has showy bracts (not petals) with a tiny true flower; maize has separate male (tassel) and female (silk/cob) inflorescences on the same plant; and passion flower has an inferior ovary with complex symmetry. We also observed that the number of stamens, the position of the ovary relative to the petals, and the presence of both or only one type of reproductive organ differed across all four specimens.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that flowers are classified by four criteria: (1) ovary position — superior (above the petals, as in Hibiscus) or inferior (below the petals, as in passion flower); (2) symmetry — actinomorphic (radially symmetrical, like Hibiscus) or zygomorphic (bilaterally symmetrical); (3) inflorescence type — solitary, raceme, spike, or panicle; and (4) whether the flower is bisexual (has both stamens and pistil) or unisexual (has only stamens or only pistil). These structural differences mean that not all flowers function the same way in reproduction.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: These structural differences in flowers help explain why a lone pawpaw or avocado tree in a Nairobi compound produces no fruit. If a flower is unisexual — having only male or only female parts — then pollen from another individual (and often from another tree entirely) is required for fertilisation to occur. Even in bisexual flowers, structural and chemical mechanisms may prevent self-pollination, which we will investigate in Lesson 3. The variation in floral structure is not random — it is shaped by the plant's reproductive strategy, which in turn determines whether a farmer needs one tree or two, one plant or many, to harvest a fruit crop.
