LESSONS.title: Who Blocked the Pollen? Mechanisms That Prevent Self-Pollination in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: protandry, protogyny, heterostyly, dioecy, self-incompatibility, cross-pollination, avocado, passion fruit, pawpaw, outbreeding

slo.purpose: By the end of this lesson, learners should be able to illustrate mechanisms and features that hinder self-pollination and self-fertilisation in plants, and present their findings to peers.
slo.knowledge: Learners will identify and describe the mechanisms — protandry, protogyny, heterostyly, dioecy, and self-incompatibility — that prevent self-pollination and self-fertilisation in flowering plants, with reference to avocado, passion fruit, pawpaw, and maize.
slo.skills: Learners will construct wire-and-bead physical models and annotate structural charts to simulate pollen movement restrictions, and will present and justify their models to peers using a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) framework.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate that biological diversity in reproductive strategies has real consequences for food security and agricultural planning in Kenya, and will prioritise collaborative model-building and peer listening during group presentations (Value: Love — prioritising others' interests).
slo.keyInquiry: How does reproduction occur in plants?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1 and 2 students established that vegetatively propagated crops (cassava, sweet potato, sugarcane) bypass the need for flowers and pollen entirely. In Lesson 2 they observed real flower specimens and classified them by floral parts. Now in Lesson 3 students confront the specific structural and biochemical 'locks' that force cross-pollination in plants like avocado and passion fruit — directly explaining why the lone pawpaw tree in the phenomenon flowers abundantly but never fruits. This lesson bridges the structural evidence of Lesson 2 to the fertilisation events of Lesson 4.
slo.safetyNotes: No sharp instruments are used in this lesson. Wire ends on bead models must be folded and taped by the teacher before distribution to prevent skin puncture. Students should not place wire pieces in their mouths. Groups handle models gently and return all components to the teacher after the lesson.

LESSONS.overview: Students begin by revisiting the phenomenon — the lone pawpaw tree that flowers but never fruits — and make a refined prediction about what structural feature of the flower might be responsible. Working in groups of 4–5, they then build wire-and-bead physical models and annotate pre-printed structural charts to simulate how protandry, protogyny, heterostyly, dioecy, and self-incompatibility physically or chemically block pollen from reaching a compatible stigma on the same plant or flower. Each group is assigned a different mechanism and presents their model to the class using a CER framework. The lesson closes with a class-wide DQB update and an exit ticket in which each student explains — in one sentence — why the lone pawpaw tree cannot fruit. Core Competencies addressed: Communication and Collaboration; Critical Thinking and Problem Solving. Value: Love. PCI: Environment and Technology.

framework.learnerExperience: Students revisit the class Driving Question Board (DQB) from Lessons 1 and 2. The teacher displays a large photograph (pre-printed or cached on screen) of a single pawpaw tree in full flower beside an image of a pawpaw tree loaded with fruit. Students individually write a prediction on a sticky note or in their exercise books in response to the prompt: 'The lone pawpaw tree has hundreds of flowers. Why does not a single flower develop into a fruit? Write one structural reason based on what you already know about flower parts.' After 3 minutes of individual writing, students share predictions with their table partner (Think-Pair). Four students are cold-called to share with the class. Teacher records key prediction words on the board (e.g., 'pollen cannot reach stigma', 'needs another tree', 'different flowers') without affirming or correcting them, telling students: 'Hold those ideas — your model today will either support or revise your prediction.'
framework.teacherMoves: Teacher displays the two pawpaw images and says verbatim: 'Before we build anything today, I want your best biological guess. Look at what you already recorded on the DQB from our last two lessons and use that to inform your prediction.' Allow 3 minutes of individual silent writing. After 3 minutes say: 'Turn to your partner — 60 seconds — compare your predictions. Find one thing you agree on and one thing you disagree on.' After paired sharing, cold-call exactly 4 students (select from different table groups, including at least one student who has not spoken in previous lessons) using: 'Akinyi, what did you and your partner agree on?' Record prediction keywords verbatim on the board in a column labelled BEFORE. Wait 12 seconds after each student speaks before responding or moving to the next student. Close with: 'Every one of these ideas is on trial today. Let your model be your evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share: Students first commit to an individual written prediction (preventing anchoring to peers' answers), then refine through paired dialogue, then hear four diverse class perspectives. This activates prior knowledge from Lessons 1–2 and creates cognitive dissonance that motivates the model-building activity. The written prediction also provides a baseline for the teacher's formative check before instruction begins.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher circulates during individual writing and reads 6–8 sticky notes or books over shoulders. Observable indicator: Can the student reference at least one structural flower feature (stamen, stigma, pollen, ovary) in their prediction? Students who write only 'it needs another tree' without structural language are flagged for targeted questioning during model-building. Teacher makes a quick mental note of the split between structural vs. non-structural predictions to inform cold-call selection.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4–5 receive a labelled kit containing: (a) a set of pre-bent wire 'stamens' (short wires) and wire 'styles' (long wires) with coloured beads representing pollen grains; (b) a pre-printed A3 structural chart showing five side-by-side flower diagrams labelled with their mechanism (Protandry – avocado Type A; Protogyny – avocado Type B; Heterostyly – passion fruit pin vs. thrum; Dioecy – pawpaw male vs. female plant; Self-incompatibility – schematic of S-locus rejection). Each group is assigned ONE mechanism. Students study their assigned diagram for 2 minutes silently, then use the wire-and-bead kit to build a 3-D model of their mechanism. Using yellow beads for pollen, they physically attempt to move pollen from the stamen wire to the style wire of the SAME flower model and record what happens (does pollen reach the stigma bead?). They then attempt the same transfer to a SECOND flower model (representing a different individual or floral type) and record the result. Students annotate their A3 chart with arrows showing: pollen source → attempted path → barrier → outcome. The teacher pre-downloaded a 3-minute animation from the Pearson Biology digital bank (cached offline) showing avocado Type A and Type B synchrony, which is shown to the whole class midway through this phase on the classroom screen or a tablet passed between groups.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute kits to groups before the lesson (set up during break to save time). Open with: 'Each group has one mechanism. You are the class experts on that mechanism — by the end of this lesson you will teach the rest of us.' Give 2 minutes for silent reading of the A3 chart, then say: 'Now build. Use the beads as pollen. Try to self-pollinate your flower model first — try to get the yellow bead from the short stamen wire onto the stigma bead of the same flower. What happens?' Circulate to each group within the first 8 minutes. At each group ask one probe: 'Show me where the barrier is in your model. Can you point to the exact structure that blocks the pollen?' Wait 10 seconds for students to respond physically with the model before speaking. At the 12-minute mark, pause all groups and play the cached avocado animation (3 minutes). After the animation, say verbatim: 'In your groups, spend 2 minutes updating your annotation — did the animation show you something your model missed? Add it in a different colour.' Cold-call 2 students from the avocado protandry group and 1 from the dioecy (pawpaw) group to verbally narrate what their model shows, asking: 'Kamau, walk us through your model — what happens when pollen tries to go to the same flower?' Wait 12 seconds after each narration before responding.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Physical model building (embodied cognition): Constructing a tangible 3-D wire-and-bead model requires students to translate abstract diagrammatic information into spatial, manipulable form. The act of physically failing to move the pollen bead to the stigma bead (because the stamen wire is too short, or the style bead is biochemically 'labelled' incompatible) creates a concrete, memorable experience of the barrier. Annotating the A3 chart simultaneously anchors the physical experience to standard scientific diagrams. The mid-activity animation provides a dynamic visual reference that students can immediately compare against their own model, prompting self-correction.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher uses an oral probe checklist (mental or clipboard): For each group, can students (a) name the mechanism, (b) identify the structural or biochemical barrier in their model, and (c) correctly predict whether self-pollination succeeds or fails? Observable indicator: Student can physically point to the barrier component in the wire model AND use the correct term. Misidentification (e.g., confusing protandry with protogyny) is corrected on the spot by asking: 'Which organ matures first in your flower — the stamen or the stigma? Check your chart.' Groups that finish early are prompted: 'Now swap models with the group next to you — can you work out their mechanism just by looking at the model?'

framework.learnerExperience: Each group presents their wire-and-bead model and annotated A3 chart to the class in a 3-minute structured presentation using the CER (Claim-Evidence-Reasoning) framework. The teacher pre-writes the CER scaffold on the board: CLAIM — 'In [plant name], self-pollination is prevented by [mechanism].' EVIDENCE — 'Our model shows that [describe what the pollen bead cannot do and why].' REASONING — 'This prevents self-fertilisation because [biological explanation].' Audience groups complete a peer review table in their exercise books: four columns labelled 'Mechanism Name', 'Plant Example', 'Structural/Biochemical Barrier', 'One Question I Have'. After all five presentations, the teacher leads a class-wide synthesis using a comparative summary table drawn on the board, asking students to volunteer entries for each mechanism row. The teacher then explicitly connects all five mechanisms back to the phenomenon: 'So which of these five mechanisms applies to our lone pawpaw tree? And which ones might explain why passion fruit on a Murang'a farm also needs a companion plant or hand-pollination to fruit?'
framework.teacherMoves: Before presentations begin, remind presenters: 'You must use the CER scaffold on the board. Every claim needs a piece of evidence from your model.' Time each group to exactly 3 minutes (use a visible timer). After each presentation, cold-call one audience student — not a volunteer — to ask one clarifying question using their peer review table: 'Otieno, you wrote a question for this group — ask it now.' Allow the presenting group 10 seconds to confer before answering. After all presentations, draw a 5-row summary table on the board (Mechanism / Plant Example / What matures first OR structural difference / Does self-pollination succeed? / Kenya agricultural consequence). Ask for volunteers to complete each cell, but cold-call at least 3 non-volunteers. Then say verbatim: 'Now look at our DQB from Lesson 1. Someone predicted the lone pawpaw needs a second tree. Which mechanism does that map onto? Put your hand up only after you have written your answer.' Wait 15 seconds, then cold-call 2 students. Write their mechanism word (Dioecy) next to the original DQB prediction card. End with: 'How does this change — or confirm — the prediction you wrote at the start of today's lesson?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) framework: Requiring students to publicly structure their explanation as Claim → Evidence → Reasoning forces them to distinguish between describing what they observed in their model (evidence) and explaining the biological mechanism (reasoning). This is an NGSS Science and Engineering Practice (Constructing Explanations). The peer review table simultaneously trains the audience in active listening and critical evaluation. The teacher-led comparative summary table then integrates all five group findings into a single coherent knowledge structure, making cross-mechanism comparisons explicit and connecting abstract mechanisms to concrete Kenyan agricultural examples (avocado in Murang'a, passion fruit farms, pawpaw in compounds).
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer review tables are collected or photographed at the end of the phase. Observable indicators: (1) Does the student correctly name all five mechanisms? (2) Does the student record a plant example for each? (3) Is the question in the fourth column a biological question (rather than a procedural question like 'how did you make the model')? Teacher also listens for CER quality during presentations: a weak response gives only a claim ('self-pollination is blocked') without mechanistic reasoning. Teacher intervenes with a scaffold prompt: 'Can you tell us what specifically about the avocado flower's timing makes that impossible?'

framework.learnerExperience: Students individually write a new sticky note (or index-card entry) for the class DQB with ONE of: (a) a revised understanding — something they now understand that they did not before this lesson; or (b) a new question — something today's lesson made them wonder about. The teacher reads selected cards aloud and physically moves earlier prediction cards on the DQB to a new column labelled 'EVIDENCE GATHERED', attaching today's mechanism names as labels. Students also update their personal science notebooks with a revised annotated diagram of the pawpaw flower, now labelling it with the correct mechanism (dioecy) and drawing an arrow showing why pollen from a male pawpaw plant cannot self-pollinate. The teacher connects today's learning forward: 'You have now shown WHY pollen cannot fertilise the same plant in these five cases. But what if the pollen does land on a compatible stigma? What happens next, inside the flower? That is the question for Lesson 4.'
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute sticky notes or ask students to write on the DQB card template in their notebooks. Say: 'You have 3 minutes — write one thing you now understand and one thing you still wonder about. Be specific — do not write
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB Model Revision: Publicly moving prediction cards to 'EVIDENCE GATHERED' makes the epistemological progress of the class visible — students can see that their earlier, imprecise predictions have been refined by evidence. Writing a personal notebook diagram immediately consolidates the lesson's central concept (dioecy in pawpaw) in visual-spatial memory. The forward-linking teacher statement creates anticipatory curiosity for Lesson 4 without closing the inquiry prematurely.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans DQB cards as they are posted. Observable indicators: (1) Are revised-understanding statements mechanistically specific (naming a mechanism) rather than vague ('I learned about flowers')? (2) Do new questions point forward toward fertilisation events (suggesting readiness for Lesson 4) or backward (suggesting unresolved gaps from today that need follow-up)? Cards with only vague statements are flagged for follow-up in the exit ticket.

framework.learnerExperience: Students individually complete a three-part exit ticket in their exercise books or on a half-sheet provided by the teacher. Part 1 (Knowledge): 'Name the mechanism that explains why the lone pawpaw tree in our phenomenon never produces fruit. Write one sentence explaining the structural reason.' Part 2 (Application): 'A passion fruit farmer in Murang'a notices that her vines flower every season but only 20% of flowers develop into fruits. She has only one variety of passion fruit. Which of the five mechanisms might explain this low fruit set? Justify your answer in two sentences.' Part 3 (Model): 'Sketch a simple diagram of either a protandrous or dioecious flower. Label the feature that prevents self-pollination and draw a dotted arrow showing the path pollen must travel to achieve cross-pollination.' Students submit exit tickets before leaving. The teacher collects and sorts them into three piles during the break: (Green) correct mechanism name + structural reason + valid sketch; (Amber) correct mechanism name but weak reasoning or missing sketch; (Red) incorrect mechanism or no structural justification.
framework.teacherMoves: Announce the exit ticket with 12 minutes remaining to allow full completion time. Say verbatim: 'This is individual — no group help. Use the vocabulary from today: protandry, protogyny, heterostyly, dioecy, self-incompatibility. I am looking for your own reasoning, not a copy of the board.' Circulate silently and do not answer content questions during this phase (redirect with: 'What does your model or chart tell you?'). Collect all exit tickets at the door or table as students leave. Before students leave, say: 'Tomorrow we follow the pollen that did make it to the right stigma. Come ready to ask: what happens inside?' Use exit ticket data tonight to identify the 4–6 students in the Red pile who need a brief re-teach at the start of Lesson 4 using a targeted question probe.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Exit ticket as formative closure: The three-part structure moves from recall (Part 1) through application to a new Kenyan agricultural context (Part 2) to diagrammatic representation (Part 3), reflecting Bloom's Taxonomy progression within a single short task. The sketch requirement (Part 3) assesses whether students can translate verbal understanding into accurate biological diagrams — a key science practice. Sorting into Green/Amber/Red piles gives the teacher actionable data for differentiated re-teaching at the start of Lesson 4.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators for Green pile: (1) Part 1 names 'dioecy' and states that male and female flowers are on separate plants so pollen cannot reach a female flower on the same individual. (2) Part 2 names 'self-incompatibility' or 'heterostyly' and provides a two-sentence biological justification referencing pollen-stigma incompatibility or pin/thrum mismatch. (3) Part 3 sketch shows at minimum: a flower outline, a labelled stamen or separate male/female plant structure, a labelled barrier feature, and a dotted arrow indicating cross-pollination direction. Teacher notes the proportion of Green/Amber/Red as a class-level indicator: if more than 40% are Red, the teacher opens Lesson 4 with a 5-minute whole-class re-teach of dioecy using the pawpaw photograph before advancing to double fertilisation.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) Did every group successfully articulate the barrier in their mechanism using correct scientific vocabulary — or did any group default to describing the model procedure without explaining the biology? If so, which mechanism caused the most confusion and how will you address it in Lesson 4's opening? (2) Were the CER presentations genuinely evidence-based — did students distinguish between model observations (evidence) and biological mechanisms (reasoning) — or did they conflate the two? Consider whether a worked CER example should be modelled explicitly at the start of the next presentation activity. (3) Did the wire-and-bead kits physically convey the right conceptual constraint? For example, did the self-incompatibility group struggle because the biochemical nature of S-locus rejection cannot easily be represented with physical materials? If so, what supplementary analogy (e.g., a 'lock-and-key' card matching activity) could replace or augment the wire model for that mechanism in future iterations? (4) Review your exit ticket Red pile: which specific mechanism was most frequently misidentified or omitted? Use this to calibrate the depth of review needed at the opening of Lesson 4. (5) Was 80 minutes sufficient for five group presentations plus model-building? If groups ran over time, consider assigning two mechanisms to stronger groups in advance so presentations can be compressed, or pre-assigning one mechanism as a flipped homework task.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Students observed physical wire-and-bead models demonstrating that pollen beads could not successfully travel from stamen wire to stigma bead in the same flower or same plant when the mechanism of protandry, protogyny, heterostyly, dioecy, or self-incompatibility was operating; they also viewed a cached animation showing avocado Type A and Type B temporal synchrony.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Students learned that five distinct structural and biochemical mechanisms — protandry (stamen matures before stigma), protogyny (stigma matures before stamen), heterostyly (pin and thrum flower types prevent same-type pollination), dioecy (male and female flowers on separate plants, as in pawpaw), and self-incompatibility (biochemical rejection of self-pollen at the stigma) — each independently block self-pollination and self-fertilisation, forcing cross-pollination and promoting genetic diversity.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: These mechanisms explain why the lone pawpaw tree in the phenomenon flowers profusely but never fruits: pawpaw is dioecious, meaning any given tree bears either male or female flowers but not both functional types on the same plant, so pollen from a male flower on one tree must reach a female flower on a separate tree for fertilisation to occur — which is impossible when only one tree is present in the compound.

LESSONS.title: Double Fertilisation: How One Pollen Grain Makes Both a Zygote and an Endosperm
LESSONS.aresKeywords: double fertilisation, pollen tube, sperm nucleus, egg cell, zygote, polar nuclei, endosperm, diploid, triploid, cross-pollination, seed formation, fruit development

slo.purpose: By the end of this lesson, learners should be able to describe the process of double fertilisation in flowering plants and link fertilisation success to seed and fruit development, thereby advancing their understanding of why cross-pollination is necessary for crops like pawpaw and avocado.
slo.knowledge: Learners will describe the sequential events of double fertilisation: pollen landing on stigma, pollen tube growth through the style, release of two sperm nuclei, fusion of one sperm with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote, and fusion of the other sperm with two polar nuclei to form a triploid endosperm nucleus.
slo.skills: Learners will watch a pre-downloaded digital animation of double fertilisation and accurately trace and diagram the fertilisation pathway — labelling the pollen tube, sperm nuclei, egg cell, zygote, polar nuclei, and endosperm — in their workbooks using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) to explain why fertilisation failure causes flower drop.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate the use of digital technology (pre-downloaded KICD-approved animations) as a tool for understanding microscopic biological processes that cannot be directly observed, connecting this to PCIs on Environment and Technology and Online Safety.
slo.keyInquiry: How does reproduction occur in plants?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This lesson is the mechanistic core of the evidence-gathering sequence. Lessons 1–3 established that cassava and sweet potato reproduce vegetatively without seeds while pawpaw and avocado require a partner tree. Lesson 4 now zooms into the cellular events of double fertilisation to explain precisely why cross-pollination is necessary — without successful fertilisation, no zygote forms, no seed develops, and the ovary cannot mature into a fruit, so the flowers drop. This understanding will anchor Lesson 5, where students examine how the fertilised ovary transforms into the fruit and seed structures they can dissect.
slo.safetyNotes: No dissecting blades or scalpels are used in this lesson. Digital devices and projector cables should be inspected before class. Students should not crowd around a single device screen; the teacher projects the animation for the whole class. If students use personal devices, the teacher must remind them to access only the pre-downloaded offline content on the ARES platform and not to browse live internet, in line with Online Safety PCI guidelines.

LESSONS.overview: Students begin by revisiting their Driving Question Board entries from Lessons 1–3 and making a written prediction about what happens inside a flower after a pollen grain lands on the stigma. The teacher then plays a pre-downloaded KICD-approved animation of pollen tube growth and double fertilisation twice — once for viewing, once for annotating a pathway diagram worksheet. Students work in groups of 4–5 to trace and label the complete fertilisation pathway in their workbooks, applying the CER framework to explain why a lone pawpaw tree drops its flowers without setting fruit. Groups share their CER statements in a whole-class discussion, and a new DQB entry is posted: 'How does the zygote and endosperm become the seed and fruit we eat?' The lesson closes with a three-question exit ticket assessing diagram accuracy and conceptual understanding of double fertilisation.

framework.learnerExperience: Students open their workbooks to the Predict section of the Lesson 4 pathway diagram worksheet. Each student individually reads the prompt on the worksheet: 'A maize pollen grain has just landed on the silk (stigma) of a maize flower on a farm in Kitale. Draw and annotate what you think happens next inside the flower before any seed can form.' Students spend 5 minutes drawing and writing their prediction silently. They then share their prediction with a partner (Think-Pair-Share) for 2 minutes, noting one similarity and one difference between their diagrams. The teacher cold-calls 4 pairs to share — selecting students who represent a range of prior knowledge including common misconceptions (e.g., that the pollen grain itself enters the ovule, or that only one nucleus is involved). Students are told their predictions will be revisited after the animation. Connection to phenomenon: Students are explicitly reminded — 'Last lesson we established that the lone pawpaw in your neighbour's compound gets pollen from somewhere — today we find out what that pollen actually does once it arrives.'
framework.teacherMoves: (0–7 min) Distribute the Lesson 4 pathway diagram worksheet before class or have it pre-loaded on ARES offline devices. Display the prediction prompt on the projector: 'A maize pollen grain has just landed on the silk (stigma) of a maize flower in Kitale. Draw and annotate what you think happens next before any seed forms.' Say verbatim: 'Work silently — I want YOUR ideas, not your neighbour's. You have 5 minutes.' Set a visible timer. After 5 minutes, say: 'Now turn to your partner and spend 2 minutes: find one thing you agree on and one thing that is different in your two diagrams.' After pairing, cold-call 4 pairs using name cards or seating chart. For each pair ask: 'What did you agree on?' then 'What was different?' Allow 10–15 seconds of WAIT TIME after each question before probing further. Record key prediction terms on the board in two columns: 'Mentions nucleus/cell fusion' vs 'No mention of nucleus.' Tell students: 'We are going to test these predictions against a KICD animation in a moment — keep your prediction visible.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share: Students first commit to an individual prediction (reducing social desirability bias), then compare with a peer to identify gaps in their own model. The teacher's two-column board record makes the class's collective prior knowledge visible, creating a cognitive anchor that the animation will confirm or challenge. This strategy activates schema for cell biology covered in earlier grades and surfaces misconceptions before instruction.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Teacher scans prediction diagrams during the 5-minute individual work period — look for whether students draw a tube structure (pollen tube) or simply draw pollen touching the ovule directly. Students who draw no tube or no nucleus label are flagged for targeted questioning during the animation phase. Cold-call responses reveal whether students recall terms such as 'nucleus,' 'ovule,' or 'fertilisation' from prior lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher plays a pre-downloaded KICD-approved animation of pollen tube growth and double fertilisation on the projector (or ARES offline platform). First viewing (3–4 min): students watch without writing, focusing on the sequence of events. The teacher pauses at three key moments and asks focus questions (see Teacher Moves). Second viewing (3–4 min): students follow along on their pathway diagram worksheet, annotating each labelled blank as the animation progresses — pollen grain, stigma, style, pollen tube, generative nucleus divides into two sperm nuclei, sperm nucleus 1 + egg cell = zygote (2n), sperm nucleus 2 + two polar nuclei = primary endosperm nucleus (3n). After the animation, students individually complete the full label set on their diagram in silence for 3 minutes. Connection to phenomenon: The animation includes a closing still image showing a pawpaw flower cross-section — the teacher points out: 'Notice the ovules in the ovary — each one needs a sperm nucleus to form a seed. Without the pollen tube reaching there, nothing happens and the flower drops — just like in our phenomenon.'
framework.teacherMoves: (8–25 min) Before playing, say: 'I am going to play this animation twice. First time — just watch, do not write. I want your eyes on the screen.' Play animation (KICD-approved, pre-downloaded). PAUSE 1 — after pollen tube begins growing: Ask: 'What is driving the pollen tube to grow downward toward the ovule?' Allow 10 seconds WAIT TIME. Cold-call 2 students. Expected answer: chemical signals / nutrients from the ovary. If no student answers correctly, say: 'The ovary releases chemical attractants — we call this chemotropism — keep watching.' PAUSE 2 — after the generative nucleus divides: Ask: 'How many sperm nuclei are now travelling down the pollen tube?' Allow 10 seconds WAIT TIME. Cold-call 2 students. PAUSE 3 — after both fusions occur: Ask: 'Two fusions just happened. Who can tell me: what fused with what in each case?' Allow 15 seconds WAIT TIME. Cold-call 3 students. Write student answers on board. Then say: 'Second viewing — this time open your worksheet to the diagram. Fill in each blank label as you see it in the animation.' Play animation again. After second viewing, say: 'Now in silence, finish labelling anything you missed. You have 3 minutes.' Circulate, looking over shoulders at diagrams — note any persistent labelling errors.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Observation with Guided Annotation: The two-pass animation strategy (watch then annotate) separates cognitive load — students are not multi-tasking during the conceptually dense first viewing. The three teacher-directed pauses with targeted questions segment the continuous animation into discrete causal steps, helping students build a sequential mental model rather than a holistic blur. This directly supports NGSS Science and Engineering Practice 2 (Developing and Using Models).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: After the second viewing, teacher circulates and checks that all seven labels on the diagram worksheet are correctly filled in (pollen grain, stigma, style, pollen tube, sperm nuclei ×2, egg cell→zygote, polar nuclei→endosperm nucleus). Students with three or more missing/incorrect labels are paired with a correctly-labelled peer during the Explain phase. The three pause-questions also serve as live oral probes — the teacher notes which students are consistently unable to answer.

framework.learnerExperience: Students remain in their groups of 4–5. Each group receives the CER framework prompt on their worksheet: 'CLAIM: State in one sentence what double fertilisation is. EVIDENCE: Cite two specific events from the animation that support your claim. REASONING: Explain how double fertilisation connects to why the lone pawpaw tree in our phenomenon drops its flowers without making fruit.' Groups have 10 minutes to construct their CER statement collaboratively. Each group nominates a spokesperson. The teacher cold-calls 4 groups to share their CER statements. The class listens and uses a peer review indicator (thumbs up / thumb sideways / thumbs down) for each statement's Reasoning component. After sharing, the teacher leads a 5-minute whole-class consolidation where the two fusion equations are written on the board: (1) Sperm nucleus 1 (n) + Egg cell (n) → Zygote (2n) — will become the embryo; (2) Sperm nucleus 2 (n) + 2 Polar nuclei (n+n) → Primary Endosperm Nucleus (3n) — will become the endosperm (food store for the seed). The teacher explicitly links this to the phenomenon: 'In a lone pawpaw tree, pollen may reach the stigma — but if it is not compatible, the pollen tube fails to grow, fertilisation never occurs, no zygote forms, and the ovary has no signal to develop into a fruit — the flower drops. A second tree of a different sex provides compatible pollen.'
framework.teacherMoves: (26–55 min) Distribute or display the CER prompt. Say verbatim: 'Your group has 10 minutes to write one Claim, two pieces of Evidence from the animation, and your Reasoning connecting fertilisation to our pawpaw phenomenon. Every person must contribute — I will ask anyone to read the Reasoning.' Set timer. Circulate to all groups — spend no more than 90 seconds per group. Prompt groups that are stuck on Reasoning with: 'Think back — what does the ovary need before it swells into a fruit? Did that happen in our lone pawpaw scenario?' After 10 minutes, cold-call 4 group spokespersons. After each CER is read, ask the class: 'Thumbs — does their Reasoning connect fertilisation to the phenomenon? Up = yes, sideways = partially, down = not yet.' Allow 10 seconds WAIT TIME for peers to decide. After 4 groups share, say: 'Let me consolidate. Watch the board.' Write the two fusion equations with ploidy numbers. Ask: 'Why does the endosperm end up with THREE sets of chromosomes — triploid?' Allow 15 seconds WAIT TIME. Cold-call 2 students. Then say: 'The endosperm is the food store — in maize grain and rice, that starchy part you eat IS the endosperm. The embryo is the tiny future plant. Both come from one pollen tube, one double fertilisation event.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) Framework: CER forces students to separate observation (evidence from the animation) from interpretation (reasoning connecting fertilisation to fruit development). The Reasoning component specifically requires students to apply mechanistic understanding to the phenomenon, not just recall facts. Peer review with thumbs provides immediate social accountability and reveals the class's collective reasoning quality to the teacher.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Teacher listens specifically for whether Reasoning statements include a causal chain — 'without pollen tube growth → no fertilisation → no zygote → no fruit development → flower drops' — rather than a simple correlation. Groups whose Reasoning omits any step in the causal chain are noted for follow-up in the DQB phase. The peer thumbs review gives the teacher a rapid whole-class read of comprehension depth.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher directs students' attention to the class Driving Question Board displayed at the front of the room (or on the ARES platform DQB digital board). Students review the entries added in Lessons 1–3. The teacher asks: 'What did we now figure out today that we did not know before?' Students individually write one 'We now know…' sticky note (or digital entry) summarising what double fertilisation explains about the phenomenon. They also write one 'We still wonder…' sticky note raising a new question prompted by today's lesson. Groups post their notes. The teacher reads several aloud, clusters related 'We still wonder' questions, and identifies the emerging question: 'How does the zygote and endosperm become the seed and fruit we see in the market?' The teacher writes this as the new DQB thread question: 'How does double fertilisation transform the ovary and ovules into the fruits and seeds we eat?' This is explicitly flagged as the focus of Lesson 5. Connection to phenomenon: The teacher points to the phenomenon recap poster: 'Today we can explain the fertilisation side of the puzzle — the lone pawpaw cannot complete double fertilisation without compatible pollen. Next lesson we follow what happens after fertilisation succeeds — how the avocado or pawpaw ovary becomes the fruit on the market stall in Wakulima Market.'
framework.teacherMoves: (56–68 min) Display or point to the DQB. Say: 'Take 2 minutes — write one We now know and one We still wonder. Be specific — use the biology terms from today.' Allow 2 minutes silent writing. Then say: 'Post your notes. If you are using ARES, type your entries now.' Collect physical sticky notes or review digital entries. Read 3–4 'We now know' entries aloud — affirm accurate ones, gently correct vague ones: 'This says 'we know pollen is important' — can we be more precise? What specifically does pollen do inside the flower?' Allow 10 seconds WAIT TIME. Cold-call 2 students to improve the statement. Then cluster 'We still wonder' notes into two categories on the board: 'About what happens AFTER fertilisation' and 'About WHY some pollen fails.' Say: 'Most of your questions are about what happens next — after fertilisation. That is exactly Lesson 5. Hold those questions — they are your investigative tools for next class.' Write the new DQB thread question visibly on the board and on ARES.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (DQB) Revision: The DQB functions as a cumulative public record of the class's growing understanding. By requiring both 'We now know' and 'We still wonder' entries, the strategy makes knowledge-building visible and models scientific practice (NGSS SEP 1: Asking Questions). Clustering student questions shows learners that their curiosity has structure — and connects their questions to the lesson sequence ahead.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: 'We now know' statements are assessed for the presence of causal language and correct biological terminology (double fertilisation, zygote, endosperm, diploid/triploid). Statements that only say 'pollen travels to the ovule' without mentioning the two fusion events signal incomplete understanding. The teacher photographs the DQB board (or screenshots digital entries) for review before Lesson 5.

framework.learnerExperience: Students return to their workbooks and open the Running Model page — a cumulative diagram of plant reproduction they have been building across all lessons in this sub-strand. In Lessons 1–3 they added structures and mechanisms (vegetative propagation, flower parts, pollination routes). Today they add the double fertilisation layer: they draw the pollen tube inside the style, label the two sperm nuclei and their fusion targets, and add two product labels — 'Zygote (2n) → embryo' and 'Primary Endosperm Nucleus (3n) → food store.' They draw a dashed arrow from the zygote and endosperm toward the ovule boundary and write: 'Ovule will become → seed (next lesson).' Students compare their updated model with a partner and check for three required elements (pollen tube drawn, both fusions labelled with ploidy, product labels present). The teacher cold-calls 3 students to describe one addition they made to their model and why. Connection to phenomenon: Students add a written annotation at the top of their running model page: 'Why the lone pawpaw fails: no compatible pollen → pollen tube fails to grow → no double fertilisation → no zygote, no endosperm → no seed signal → flower drops.'
framework.teacherMoves: (69–78 min) Say: 'Open your running model page. You have 6 minutes to add today's double fertilisation events to your cumulative diagram. You must include: (1) pollen tube drawn inside the style, (2) both fusion reactions labelled with ploidy numbers, (3) the two products labelled. Ready — start.' Set timer. Circulate — spend 30 seconds at 6–8 desks, checking for the three required elements. If a student is missing ploidy numbers, ask quietly: 'How many chromosome sets does the zygote have? Why?' Allow 10 seconds WAIT TIME before providing a hint. After 6 minutes, say: 'Compare with your partner — does their model have all three required elements? Tick them off together.' Allow 2 minutes peer check. Cold-call 3 students: 'Tell me one thing you added to your model and why it matters for explaining our phenomenon.' Allow 10–12 seconds WAIT TIME per student. Affirm accurate additions. Conclude by saying: 'Your model is growing. Today we understand fertilisation. Lesson 5 — we follow what those zygote and endosperm cells become: the seed and fruit inside that avocado or passion fruit you buy at the market.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: The running model strategy (NGSS SEP 2) requires students to integrate each new lesson's evidence into a single evolving diagram rather than producing isolated lesson notes. The three-element peer check introduces low-stakes accountability and distributed feedback. The phenomenon annotation at the top of the model page ensures that mechanistic detail stays tethered to the real-world puzzle — preventing the model from becoming a decontextualised biology diagram.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Teacher checks that all three required model elements are present and correctly labelled during circulation. The peer-check provides a second pass. Cold-call responses reveal whether students can articulate the causal significance of their additions (not just label them). Students whose models are missing ploidy numbers or whose cold-call responses lack causal language are flagged for the Lesson 5 review warm-up.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did students' CER Reasoning statements include the full causal chain from fertilisation failure to flower drop — or did they stop at 'no fertilisation'? If the causal chain was incomplete for more than one-third of groups, build a 5-minute review of the chain into the Lesson 5 warm-up. (2) Were students able to correctly assign ploidy numbers (2n for zygote, 3n for endosperm) in their running models, or did they confuse the two products? If confusion persists, draw the two fusion equations again at the start of Lesson 5 before introducing fruit development. (3) Did the pre-downloaded animation play without technical interruption? If devices failed, note which groups used paper diagrams only and ensure they receive a printed animation screenshot handout before Lesson 5. (4) Did any student raise an interesting 'We still wonder' question beyond seed and fruit development — such as questions about why some plants self-fertilise and others do not? These questions connect to the mechanisms lesson already covered (Lesson 3) and can be validated as good scientific thinking without derailing the sequence. (5) Reflect on equity: in a class of 45–50, were quieter students given cold-call opportunities, or did the same confident voices dominate? Review your cold-call record and ensure all four lesson phases included at least one student from rows at the back of the room.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Students watched a pre-downloaded KICD-approved animation of pollen tube growth and double fertilisation, pausing at three key moments to answer oral probe questions. They annotated a pathway diagram worksheet during a second viewing, labelling seven structures and events from stigma to endosperm nucleus formation.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Double fertilisation involves two simultaneous fusion events inside the ovule: (1) one sperm nucleus fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote (2n), which will develop into the embryo; and (2) a second sperm nucleus fuses with two polar nuclei to form a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (3n), which will develop into the food store of the seed. Without successful pollen tube growth and double fertilisation, no zygote or endosperm forms, so no seed develops and the ovary cannot mature into a fruit — explaining why the lone pawpaw in the phenomenon drops its flowers.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: In our phenomenon, cross-pollination from a second compatible pawpaw or avocado tree is necessary because compatible pollen is the prerequisite for pollen tube growth, which is the prerequisite for double fertilisation, which is the prerequisite for seed and fruit development. A lone tree may flower, but without compatible pollen completing the double fertilisation process, the ovary receives no developmental signal and the flower abscises (drops). Crops like cassava and sweet potato bypass this entire process through vegetative propagation, which is why they produce offspring reliably without pollen, fertilisation, or seeds.

LESSONS.title: Cracking Open the Evidence: Fruit Dissection and Placentation Classification
LESSONS.aresKeywords: placentation, axile, marginal, parietal, free-central, fruit development, seed arrangement, fertilisation, ovary, dissection

slo.purpose: Students will section, examine, draw, and label local fruits to classify placentation types and understand seed arrangement as direct anatomical evidence of fertilisation and ovary development.
slo.knowledge: Students will know that: (1) fruits develop from the ovary after fertilisation; (2) seeds develop from ovules after fertilisation; (3) the four main placentation types — marginal, axile, parietal, and free-central — describe where ovules are attached inside the ovary; (4) each local fruit specimen (orange, bean pod, tomato, passion fruit, cucumber) exhibits a distinct and identifiable placentation pattern.
slo.skills: Students will be able to: (1) safely use a scalpel or razor blade to make transverse and longitudinal sections of fresh fruits; (2) accurately draw and label biological diagrams of fruit cross-sections; (3) classify fruits by placentation type using observable evidence; (4) construct a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) argument linking seed arrangement to post-fertilisation ovary development.
slo.attitudes: Students will appreciate the value of sharing dissecting equipment and specimens equitably across group members (Social Justice value); students will approach practical work with care and precision, recognising that biological evidence requires careful observation rather than assumption.
slo.keyInquiry: How does reproduction occur in plants?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In previous lessons students established how pollen travels, how double fertilisation occurs, and how seeds form. This lesson provides the culminating anatomical proof: students physically open real Kenyan fruits — orange, tomato, passion fruit, bean pod, cucumber — and see with their own hands that seeds sit precisely where ovules were attached inside the ovary. This transforms fertilisation from an abstract animation into visible, touchable evidence, and directly advances the driving question by showing that seed-bearing fruits are the product of successful sexual reproduction, explaining why the lone pawpaw or avocado in the farmer's compound flowers but never fruits without a pollen donor nearby.
slo.safetyNotes: EXPLICIT LAB SAFETY PROTOCOL — Lesson 5: (1) All scalpels and single-sided razor blades must be distributed handle-first by the teacher or lab technician only — students must never reach into the equipment box. (2) Students must place the fruit firmly on the dissecting tray or cutting board before cutting; never cut toward the hand or fingers. (3) Only one cutting motion per fruit specimen at a time; the student holding the fruit must withdraw their hand before any cut is made. (4) Blades must be laid flat on the tray (never handed blade-first between students) when not in use. (5) Any student with a cut must report immediately; first-aid kit location must be announced at lesson start. (6) Fruit juice and pulp can cause slipping — wipe trays with paper towel regularly. (7) Students with latex allergies should be identified before handling passion fruit or cucumber skins. (8) Dispose of fruit waste in the bin provided, not on the floor. (9) Wash hands thoroughly after dissection before touching face or eyes.

LESSONS.overview: This 80-minute practical lesson sits at the heart of the evidence-gathering sequence. Students begin by predicting the internal arrangement of seeds in five common Kenyan fruits, then systematically dissect, observe, draw, and label cross-sections to classify four placentation types. A Think-Pair-Share bridges the observation to a whole-class Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) activity that connects seed arrangement to the process of fertilisation explored in Lesson 4. The lesson closes with a Driving Question Board update and a model revision in which students annotate their cumulative reproduction diagrams with the post-fertilisation fate of the ovary. The Social Justice value is embedded through deliberate, teacher-monitored equitable resource distribution across groups of 4–5. All animations from Lesson 4 remain cached on devices for reference. Exit ticket: a labeled diagram of one assigned fruit cross-section plus a one-sentence CER claim.

framework.learnerExperience: Students sit in pre-assigned groups of 4–5 (maximum 10 groups for a class of 45–50). Each group receives a Predict Sheet showing five unlabelled outlines of fruit cross-sections (orange, tomato, bean pod, passion fruit, cucumber). Without opening any fruit, students individually sketch where they think seeds will be found inside each fruit, and write one sentence explaining their reasoning for each. They then share predictions within their group and agree on a 'group consensus prediction' to display on their mini-whiteboards or rough paper held up to the teacher. Students connect their prediction to the driving question by answering: 'If these seeds exist because of fertilisation, what does that tell us about the pawpaw tree that never fruits?'
framework.teacherMoves: Teacher posts the lesson anchor question on the board: 'What does the inside of a fruit tell us about what happened to the ovary after fertilisation?' Teacher distributes Predict Sheets (pre-printed or written on board for students to copy). Teacher says verbatim: 'Before we cut anything open, I want your honest best guess — not the right answer, your reasoning. You have 3 minutes to sketch individually, then 2 minutes to agree in your group.' After 5 minutes, teacher cold-calls 3 groups (Groups 2, 5, and 8) to share their consensus predictions using the prompt: 'Group 2 — show me your whiteboard and tell me in one sentence WHY you placed the seeds there.' Teacher applies 10-second WAIT TIME after each group responds before moving on. Teacher records 3–4 contrasting group predictions visibly on the board under the heading 'Our Predictions' — these remain visible throughout the lesson for later comparison. Teacher does NOT correct predictions at this stage.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) — Phase 1 (Predict): By committing predictions to paper before observation, students activate prior knowledge from Lessons 3 and 4 (ovule position, double fertilisation) and create a cognitive conflict that the dissection will resolve. Keeping predictions visible builds metacognitive awareness of how evidence changes thinking.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every student has a completed individual Predict Sheet with at least one reasoning sentence per fruit before group sharing begins. Teacher circulates and scans sheets — look specifically for students who confuse 'seed' with 'fruit flesh' or who predict all fruits have the same internal structure. These students are flagged for targeted cold-calling during the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Safety briefing (3 minutes): Teacher delivers explicit lab safety protocol verbatim from safety notes. Students repeat the two cardinal rules chorally: 'Blade on tray, not in hand' and 'Fruit on board before I cut.' Each group of 4–5 receives: one dissecting tray, one scalpel or single-sided razor blade (distributed handle-first by teacher), one hand lens, paper towels, and an allocated fruit specimen set. To manage equitable access, each group member is assigned a role by the teacher: Cutter (makes the sections), Holder (stabilises the tray — NOT the fruit during cutting), Recorder (draws diagrams), Observer 1 (examines with hand lens), Observer 2 / Reporter (reports to class). Roles rotate every 10 minutes so each student handles each fruit. Students make BOTH a transverse (cross) section and a longitudinal section of each fruit, placing both halves on the tray. Students observe: number of locules (chambers), position of seeds, the tissue to which seeds are attached (the placenta). Students complete a structured Observation Table in their notebooks: Fruit | Section type | Number of locules | Seed position | Tissue seeds attach to | Placentation type (to be confirmed). Students sketch each cross-section as a biological diagram: outline in pencil, label lines drawn with ruler, no shading, magnification noted.
framework.teacherMoves: Teacher circulates continuously using a 3-minute rotation pattern across 10 groups. At each group teacher asks one targeted question from this list (rotate questions): (1) 'Show me exactly where the seeds attach — touch the tissue with your pencil tip.' (2) 'How many chambers do you count? Are seeds in ALL chambers or only some?' (3) 'Compare your tomato cross-section to your orange cross-section — what is the SAME and what is DIFFERENT about where seeds sit?' (4) 'You said seeds are in the middle — is that true for the bean pod too? Look again.' Teacher applies 12-second WAIT TIME after each question before offering a follow-up prompt. At the 15-minute mark teacher pauses the class with a hand signal and cold-calls 2 groups (different from Predict phase — Groups 1 and 6): 'Group 1 — hold up your bean pod cross-section drawing. Tell me in one sentence where the seeds are.' Teacher explicitly narrates the equitable resource sharing: 'I can see Group 3 is letting only one person use the hand lens — please pass it around now so everyone observes. This is our Social Justice value in action: shared resources, shared understanding.' Teacher reminds students at the 20-minute mark to rotate roles. Teacher points to the 'Our Predictions' board periodically: 'Is what you are seeing matching what you predicted? If not, note that discrepancy in your table.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) — Phase 2 (Observe): Direct hands-on observation of real Kenyan fruits creates perceptual evidence that cannot be dismissed. The structured Observation Table scaffolds noticing — students are directed to look at specific features (locules, seed attachment tissue) rather than making undirected observations, increasing the quality of evidence they gather for the subsequent Explain phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each student's notebook contains a biologically accurate diagram of at least two fruit cross-sections with at least three label lines drawn with a ruler before the Explain phase begins. (2) The Observation Table is at least 60% complete. Teacher does a rapid 'diagram check' — circulating and placing a tick on tables that have ruler-drawn label lines and pencil outlines. Students without ruler-drawn diagrams are redirected immediately: 'Biology diagrams must have ruled label lines — correct this before we move to the next phase.'

framework.learnerExperience: Think-Pair-Share (8 minutes): Students individually re-examine their Observation Table and attempt to complete the 'Placentation type' column using a Reference Card provided by the teacher. The Reference Card contains: four placentation type names, a one-line definition, and a simple diagram of each (marginal — seeds on the inner wall along one suture, as in bean pod; axile — seeds on a central column where partition walls meet, as in orange and tomato; parietal — seeds on the outer wall in a one-chambered ovary, as in passion fruit and cucumber; free-central — seeds on a central column with no partitions). After 4 minutes individual work, students pair with a group neighbour to compare classifications and resolve disagreements by returning to their fruit specimens. Pairs share their final classification with the group. Whole-class CER activity (14 minutes): Teacher writes on the board: CLAIM: 'Fruits and seeds develop from the ovary and ovules after fertilisation, and the position of seeds reveals the placentation type of the original ovary.' Teacher explains the CER framework verbatim: 'Your CLAIM is the statement you are defending. Your EVIDENCE is the specific observation from your dissection — name the fruit, the section, what you saw. Your REASONING is the biological explanation that links your evidence to the claim using the words ovary, ovule, fertilisation, and locule.' Groups have 6 minutes to write one CER paragraph collectively in their notebooks. Teacher then cold-calls 4 groups (Groups 3, 4, 7, 10) to read their CER aloud. After each group reads, teacher asks the class: 'Thumbs up if you agree with their reasoning, sideways if you are unsure, down if you disagree.' Teacher addresses one 'thumbs sideways or down' response per group with the prompt: 'What would you change in their reasoning to make it stronger?' — applying 10-second WAIT TIME before taking a response. Teacher connects back to the driving question: 'So — if a single pawpaw or avocado tree flowers but the ovules are never fertilised, what does today's dissection tell us about why no fruit develops? Turn and tell your partner in 15 seconds.' Cold-calls 2 pairs to share.
framework.teacherMoves: Teacher distributes Reference Cards at the start of the Explain phase. Teacher writes CER scaffold on board and leaves it visible throughout. During Think-Pair-Share, teacher targets the 3–4 students flagged during the Predict phase for individual check-ins: 'Show me your classification for passion fruit — walk me through your reasoning.' Teacher uses the 'Thumbs' protocol as a whole-class formative check after each group's CER reading. Teacher explicitly names the reasoning words students must use: 'I need to hear the words OVULE and FERTILISATION in your reasoning — if they are not there, the reasoning is incomplete.' Teacher re-displays the driving question poster: 'WHY do some farm plants produce offspring without seeds while others require seeds and a partner tree to make fruit?' and says: 'Every CER you write today is a piece of evidence that answers part of this question.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share followed by Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER): Think-Pair-Share surfaces misconceptions at the pair level before whole-class exposure, reducing public embarrassment and increasing participation. CER formalises the link between observation and explanation by requiring students to explicitly state why their evidence supports the claim — this is the core sensemaking move that transforms 'I saw seeds in the middle' into 'The axile placentation of the orange cross-section is evidence that the ovules were attached to the central axis of the ovary, which developed into the fruit after fertilisation.'
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each group's CER paragraph contains all three components, includes at least one specific fruit name and section type as evidence, and uses the words 'ovary,' 'ovule,' and 'fertilisation' in the reasoning. (2) During Thumbs protocol, teacher notes which concepts attract the most 'sideways' or 'down' responses — these are flagged for re-teaching in Lesson 6. (3) Cold-called pairs can articulate in one sentence why a lone pawpaw tree cannot produce fruit, using the word 'fertilisation.'

framework.learnerExperience: Each group receives two sticky notes of different colours (e.g., green = new understanding, orange = new question). On the GREEN note, the group writes one specific thing they now understand about the driving question that they did not understand before this lesson — it must reference placentation or fruit development. On the ORANGE note, the group writes one new question that today's dissection has raised that remains unanswered — this should connect to the next lesson's focus on advantages/disadvantages of sexual vs asexual reproduction. Groups place their sticky notes on the class DQB under the appropriate columns: 'We now understand…' and 'We still wonder…'. Two volunteers read aloud one green and one orange note each. Teacher highlights one orange note that directly previews Lesson 6: 'This question — [reads student note] — is exactly what we will investigate next lesson.'
framework.teacherMoves: Teacher says: 'Our Driving Question Board tracks how our thinking grows across all 8 lessons. Today's dissection gave us new evidence — let's update the board to show what we now know and what we still need to figure out.' Teacher ensures every group places BOTH sticky notes on the board before the phase ends. Teacher reads two contrasting green notes aloud and asks: 'How do these two understandings connect to each other?' — applying 10-second WAIT TIME. Teacher physically draws an arrow on the DQB between the Lesson 4 'double fertilisation' notes and today's 'placentation' notes, narrating: 'Double fertilisation in Lesson 4 → ovule becomes seed, ovary becomes fruit → seed position reveals placentation type. These ideas are connected.' Teacher previews Lesson 6 using the orange sticky notes without giving away the answer.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (DQB) revision: The DQB makes the progression of understanding visible and cumulative. By physically connecting today's sticky notes to Lesson 4 entries, the teacher models how scientific knowledge builds — each lesson's evidence does not stand alone but advances the collective explanation of the phenomenon. This metacognitive strategy helps students see themselves as scientists building an explanation over time.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every group's green sticky note makes a specific reference to placentation, fruit development, or seed arrangement — generic statements such as 'we learned about fruits' are sent back for revision with the prompt: 'Be specific — which placentation type did you see, and in which fruit?'

framework.learnerExperience: Students return to their cumulative Reproduction Model — a diagram they have been building and annotating across Lessons 1–4 showing the progression from flower structure through pollination, double fertilisation, and now fruit and seed development. Using coloured pencils, students add a new annotated layer to their model: (1) They draw a simplified cross-section of ONE fruit of their choice from today's dissection and label: ovary wall (now pericarp/fruit wall), locules, placenta, seeds (from ovules), and placentation type. (2) They draw a connecting arrow from 'fertilised ovule' in their Lesson 4 model section to 'seed' in today's new section, and from 'ovary' to 'fruit.' (3) They write a caption beneath the new model section: 'After fertilisation, the ovary of [chosen fruit] developed into a fruit with [placentation type] placentation, housing seeds that formed from fertilised ovules.' Students then turn to their partner and explain their model diagram aloud in 60 seconds — partner listens and must ask one clarifying question.
framework.teacherMoves: Teacher says: 'Your model has been growing since Lesson 1. Today you are adding the final post-fertilisation step — what actually happens to the ovary and ovules AFTER the double fertilisation you animated last lesson. Add this to your model now.' Teacher circulates and conducts oral probes with 4–5 individual students: (1) 'Point to where the seed came from in your model and explain using the words ovule and fertilisation.' (2) 'If the ovary of a passion fruit has parietal placentation, where would you expect to find seeds in your model — on the central axis or on the outer wall?' (3) 'Your model shows a bean pod — which placentation type is that? How does this connect to why bean pods split along one edge when dry?' Teacher applies 12-second WAIT TIME after each oral probe before offering scaffolding. Teacher collects 5 randomly selected student models (not announced in advance) for review between lessons — these inform the start of Lesson 6.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Building: Requiring students to physically add today's evidence to a diagram that spans all previous lessons forces integration rather than isolated recall. The 60-second partner explanation (a peer-teaching micro-routine) consolidates understanding through verbalisation — students who can explain their model to a peer with a clarifying question have achieved deeper encoding than students who merely label a diagram.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) The new model section contains all five required labels (pericarp, locules, placenta, seeds, placentation type name) with ruled label lines. (2) Connecting arrows are drawn from the Lesson 4 fertilisation section to today's fruit development section. (3) During oral probes, the student can use the words 'ovule,' 'ovary,' 'fertilisation,' and the specific placentation type name in a single coherent sentence without teacher prompting. (4) The partner's clarifying question is recorded in the student's notebook next to the model — this is checked during the collected model review.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) SAFETY: Were all blades accounted for at the end of the practical? Did any student attempt to pass a blade hand-to-hand rather than setting it on the tray? What will you adjust in the safety briefing for any future practical lessons? (2) EQUITY: Did all group members rotate roles during dissection? Were there groups where one student dominated the scalpel? How did you intervene or will you intervene next time? (3) EVIDENCE QUALITY: Could students articulate the difference between marginal and parietal placentation using their own specimen as evidence, or did they rely solely on the Reference Card? If many relied on the card, consider adding a third cross-section drawing to the next dissection lesson. (4) CER QUALITY: Did student CER paragraphs include genuine reasoning (linking ovule position to fertilisation) or were they mostly re-stating observations as claims? If reasoning was weak, plan a 5-minute CER 'anchor chart' warm-up at the start of Lesson 6. (5) DQB CONNECTION: Did the orange sticky notes genuinely raise questions about sexual vs asexual reproduction trade-offs, or were they superficial? If superficial, the phenomenon context (lone pawpaw, cassava stem cutting) may need to be re-anchored at the start of Lesson 6. (6) COLLECTED MODELS: Review the 5 collected cumulative models before Lesson 6. Check specifically: are connecting arrows present from fertilisation to fruit development? Are placentation type names correctly matched to fruit specimens? Use errors to design the first 5 minutes of Lesson 6.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Students sectioned and examined fresh local fruits — orange, tomato, bean pod, passion fruit, and cucumber — making both transverse and longitudinal cuts, then observed and recorded the number of locules, the position of seeds, and the tissue to which seeds are attached in each specimen.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Fruits develop from the ovary and seeds develop from ovules after fertilisation; seeds are arranged according to the placentation type of the original ovary — marginal (bean pod), axile (orange, tomato), parietal (passion fruit, cucumber) — and these patterns are direct anatomical evidence of the post-fertilisation development of the flower's ovary.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Because a lone pawpaw or avocado tree produces flowers but no fruit, and today's dissection showed that seeds and fruit only develop from ovules and ovary tissue AFTER fertilisation, the lone tree's flowers must be dropping off because fertilisation is not occurring — meaning pollen from another individual is required. This is why Kenyan farmers who plant a second pawpaw or avocado nearby suddenly get fruit: the ovules are now being fertilised, so the ovary develops into a fruit containing seeds arranged in its characteristic placentation pattern.
